data: Butler left his books in his study and chose instead to observe and listen to bees in the field. We are particularly interested in his study of swarms. We hope that today's beekeepers can add their knowledge to our project.

They might be tangential to our main topic, or an aside that seems pertinent enough to be recorded. Some of these buzzwords might turn into longer articles, others will remain here as a fleeting reflection.

Cool Tunes For a Hot Planet Podcast

Produced by a team of like-minded musician/activists, the podcast explores the intersection of music and the struggle for social and environmental justice. The 'bees' episode grew from a belief that music from multiple places and times, but centered around universal human experiences, would create compelling and meaningful programming
Thought experiment: a queen bee in interdisciplinary space

We've been looking at how this book thinks with bees, and how the writing uses all these modes to move around the bees creating emotional insight. Its polyphony is a prompt and a challenge. The many elements of the book naturally worked together in Butler's mind, but in 2024 they are distributed between specialisms in the departments of the university. Revisiting Butler's book with a team representing the different strands of his thinking offers a unique chance to see how what we now call 'interdisciplinarity' works

A film about bees and bee keeping
*Where the Bee Sucks* is a 50 min film that looks at the year long cycle of bee keeping from the point of view of Ralph, the bee keeper.
A screen grab from Where the Bee Sucks, depicting the beekeeper, Ralph, tending to his hives dressed in a green smock and face veil.

The idea that we are entering a 'hive' when we open the 1623 edition is also suggested by this work’s material features, indicating Butler’s collaboration with the printer, Haviland. One of those features meets us as soon as we open the book: the new woodcut facing the titlepage.

The honey bee: a conscious bee-ing?

Bees are a flagship species in the study of invertebrate consciousness. Beloved by the public for their ecological importance and complex social behaviors, they provide a unique opportunity to engage society in the broader discussion about animal consciousness.

Here you will find the raw data for some of the experiments we ran in the bee lab, for you to explore in various forms, validate our interpretations, and draw your own conclusions.

The study of emotions in invertebrates has been a subject of both intrigue and scepticism. While challenging our anthropocentric notions, the investigation of emotions in invertebrates promises to broaden the understanding of the evolutionary origins and adaptive functions of these phenomena across the animal kingdom.

Prior to joining Cambridge in 2023, Jennifer (FBA, FEA) was the Joseph Cowen Chair, Newcastle University, and the Director of the Humanities Research Institute.  Her areas of expertise include Renaissance English Literature, the history of reading, history of rhetoric (with a focus on delivery), and scholarly editing. Her most recent book, *Voices and Books in the English Renaissance: A New History of Reading*, was published by Oxford in 2019. It was out of this work on voice, rhetoric and reading that her interest in Charles Butler's study of the sound of bees began. As Chair of the English Association, and in collaboration with the School of Advanced Studies, London, she has launched an online series exploring collaboration: ['Thinking Forwards'](https://englishassociation.ac.uk/thinking-forwards-collaboration/).

Olivia Smith works on early modern literature, with a focus on natural history and science writing, and histories of emotion and cognition. Before coming to Cambridge, she was Balzan Research Fellow and then Wellcome Trust Research Fellow at Oxford. She has devised masterclasses at the Royal College of Physicians and in the Wellcome archive, and is interested in articulating the value of a humanities skillset across the disciplines. With colleagues in Modern Languages she's co-edited the books *Cognitive Confusions: Dreams, Delusions and Illusions in Early Modern Culture* (2017) and the forthcoming *Elemental Objects: Proceedings from a Virtual Showcase* (2025). Her most recently published essay is a piece on the early modern condition of erotomania, which appears in *Love: A Cultural History*, edited by Katherine Ibbett (2024).

John Doe is a seasoned professional with over 20 years of experience in the technology industry. He holds a Masters degree in Computer Science from the University of Technology and has worked with several leading tech companies throughout his career. John specializes in software development, project management, and IT consulting. He has a proven track record of delivering high-quality software solutions on time and within budget. John is passionate about mentoring young professionals and has been a guest speaker at numerous tech conferences. In his free time, he enjoys hiking, reading, and exploring new technologies.

Magnus Williamson (FSA) researches the musical traditions of late-medieval and early modern Europe, especially in the sources and contexts of early-Tudor polyphony. He has led and participated in a number of collaborative projects: the Early English Organ Project; the *Experience of Worship* (AHRC/ESRC, 2009-12); *Dispositifs de la Performance Musicale à la Renaissance* (CNRS/Le Studium, 2013-14); *Tudor Partbooks* (AHRC, 2014-17); *Tallis* (Leverhulme Trust, visiting fellowship, 2017); the *Sarum Hymnal in Manuscript and Print* (British Academy, 2017-18); *English Saints Offices* (British Academy, 2029-21); *Aural Histories* (AHRC, 2022-25); *Henry VIII on Tour* (2022-25) and *Bee-ing Human* (Leverhulme Trust, 2022-25).  His facsimile edition of the Eton Choirbook (Oxford, 2010) won the American Musicological Society’s Palisca Prize. He is chairman of the British Academy edition, Early English Church Music.

Tiago is a frontend web developer and digital humanist. Before his graduate and post-graduate education in literature, he worked as a software developer and studied computer engineering in Portugal. Between 2017 and 2021, he was the Research Associate for the *[ATNU](https://research.ncl.ac.uk/atnu/)* project, based at the School of English, where he also taught literary and digital humanities’ focused modules. In 2020-2021, he convened and ran the *Coding for Humanists* study group, and from 2022 he is one of the co-convenors of the *Code Community* at Newcastle University. Until 2022 he was a co-managing editor of the *[Journal of the Text Encoding Initiative](https://journals.openedition.org/jtei/)* and an editorial assistant for *[The Programming Historian](https://programminghistorian.org/en/)*

Vivek Nityananda received his PhD from the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru. He worked in Minneapolis and London before moving to Newcastle University where he is now a Senior Lecturer. He researches insect vision, cognition and welfare. He is also interested in pessimism and optimism and has written a book on overconfidence. He collaborates with researchers in the arts and humanities and regularly communicates science through cartoons, animation and plays.
Newcastle University and University of Turin

Luigi Baciadonna has a background in psychology and obtained his PhD in Biological Sciences from Queen Mary University of London in 2017. His research focuses on the expression and perception of emotions across different animal species, ranging from insects to vertebrates. After almost a decade in the UK he moved to Italy to work on the cognitive and perceptual abilities in African penguins. In 2022, he was awarded a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship (FEAR-BEES) to conduct a European project on the neurobiological mechanisms of fear in honey bees at the French CNRS (IBPS - Paris Sorbonne & CBI-CRCA - Paul Sabatier University) and the University of Florence (Italy). His work integrates behavioural, cognitive and neurophysiological approaches to explore how emotions shape cognition and decision-making in animals.
Institute of Biology Paris, Seine - Sorbonne University Paris

Martin Giurfa is an Exceptional-Class Professor of Neurosciences at Sorbonne University, where he directs the Institute of Biology Paris-Seine. His research focuses on learning, memory and cognitive processing in insects, from behavior to molecules. He has brought a cognitive dimension to studies on honey bee learning and memory as his work revealed bees under the new light of their remarkable cognitive faculties.
CNRS - NeuroSU, Institute of Biology Paris Seine

Catherine Macri - Doctoral Candidate, CNRS - NeuroSU, Institute of Biology Paris Seine, Sorbonne university & Research Center on Animal Cognition, University of Toulouse - Investigates markers of consciousness (such as perceptual awareness and fear) in honey bees, at the behavioral, physiological and neurobiological level.

Born in London 1948,  I was a post-war boy child with a GI dad and a Yorkshire mum, I went to St Pauls School in London and attended first Sussex University then Cambridge where respectively I studied Sociology and Criminology.  After University I worked as a lecturer at Newcastle Polytechnic (now Northumbria University) but never felt that teaching was right for me.  I gave it up and embarked on a life in the theatre founding and developing local NE companies such as Mamon Theatre Group and Skin and Bones.  Seeing the films of Godard in the 1960’s showed me anyone could make a film if they really wanted. I started to make films in standard 8 and super 8 systems, eventually teaching myself 16mm skills and from the 1980’s to date have made some 16 documentaries (some of which can be found at www.crinklecut.co.uk )   many of which concentrate on the practice of work.

Warren Senders is a musician, educator, and activist living outside of Boston in the city of Medford, Massachusetts. He is a faculty member at New England Conservatory of Music, and a scholar/performer specializing in North Indian (Hindustani) classical singing.
His work in climate activism began in 2009. Since then, he has:
  • Produced a series of 21 semi-annual benefit concerts for [350.org](https://www.350.org) and [350MA.org](http://www.350MA.org), under the heading, 'Playing For The Planet: World Music Against Climate Change.'
    • [https://artsfuse.org/45084/fuse-music-feature-playing-for-the-planet/](https://artsfuse.org/45084/fuse-music-feature-playing-for-the-planet/)
    • [https://www.bostoncentral.com/events/music/p62785.php](https://www.bostoncentral.com/events/music/p62785.php)
    The concert series came to a close at the beginning of the pandemic.
  • Curated 45 hours of streaming music videos and interviews during the 2021 Glasgow COP as the Programming Director of **Music For Climate Justice** (M4CJ). The programming included over 450 different artists in an exceptionally wide range of musical genres and performances centered on environmental awareness and justice. The 'Music For Climate Justice Video Festival' was almost certainly the most diverse musical event in history, featuring artists ranging from Pete Seeger to John Cage, from underwater video recorded in Antarctica to the voices of astronauts in the ISS, from Terje Isungset's instruments made of glacial ice to the 'pyrophones' of fire musician Michel Moglia.
    • [https://events.music4climatejustice.org/en/](https://events.music4climatejustice.org/en/)
    • [https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/bootsy-collins-steven-van-zandt-music4climatejustice-festival-1252340/](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/bootsy-collins-steven-van-zandt-music4climatejustice-festival-1252340/)
    • [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=daC9CT4G-ig](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=daC9CT4G-ig)
  • Written 1461 climate-focused letters to the editor between January 1, 2010 and December 31, 2014 — one letter a day for four years to newspapers, magazines, and journals. Letters were published all over the world; US appearances included the New York Times, Washington Post, Time Magazine, USA Today, and many regional newspapers/magazines.
    • [Sample letter published in the Portland Press-Herald, 12/29/2013](https://www.pressherald.com/2013/12/29/letters_to_the_editor__lepage_wrong_to_embrace_climate_change_as_potential_profit_center/)
    • [Sample letter published in the Cleveland Plain Dealer, November 15, 2013](https://www.cleveland.com/letters/2013/11/letter_to_the_editor_365.html)
  • Maintains a daily 'Climate Vigil' at Roosevelt Circle in Medford, a heavily-trafficked intersection near his home. He and vigil partner Craige Knopf stand with signs about climate change for one hour every weekday morning between 7:30-8:30. Articles have been written about this ongoing action (2015-present) in the US and India:
    • [https://www.thehindu.com/news/cities/mumbai/entertainment/man-with-sign-and-raga/article8383653.ece?ref=tpnews](https://www.thehindu.com/news/cities/mumbai/entertainment/man-with-sign-and-raga/article8383653.ece?ref=tpnews)
    • [https://orionmagazine.org/article/protest-as-practice/](https://orionmagazine.org/article/protest-as-practice/)
    • [https://indianexpress.com/article/express-sunday-eye/notes-from-a-dying-planet-5574200/](https://indianexpress.com/article/express-sunday-eye/notes-from-a-dying-planet-5574200/)
  • Was part of the West Roxbury 13, whose civil disobedience in blocking a LNG Pipeline led to the first successful US use of the Necessity Defense.
    • [http://www.ililani.media/2018/04/climate-activists-successfully-relied.html](http://www.ililani.media/2018/04/climate-activists-successfully-relied.html)
    • [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hZdMZ5fTsQs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hZdMZ5fTsQs)
    He has been arrested for NVCD several times in the years since then, mostly through Extinction Rebellion's Boston chapter.
  • Mr. Senders teaches a course at New England Conservatory in which students make their own instruments from recycled & trash materials, thereby transforming their understanding of, and relationship to, the consumer economy and the waste stream.
    • [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tuY6GCk1UNc](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tuY6GCk1UNc)
  • He prepared this personal summary for the political blog 'Balloon-Juice' almost exactly a year ago:
    • [https://balloon-juice.com/2024/01/06/warren-senders-music-and-conscience/](https://balloon-juice.com/2024/01/06/warren-senders-music-and-conscience/)
